According to mythology, the Korwa tribe originated from the womb (Kora in their language) of a 
virgin goddess called Matha Koithama. It was in Ratanpur, when all the gods and goddess gathered 
together, that Matha Koithama, although being a virgin, gave birth to a baby.1 Since he was born in 
the presence of gods, this baby was known as Korwa (Powercity Korba n.d.c).

According to another legend, the Korwa were created when god created man (the word kor 
means ‘man’). It is plausible that there is a relation between the word kor and the etymology of the 
word Korwa (Singh 1994:1826). Another source says that the Korwa tribe believe themselves to be a 
member of the Kauravs of Mahabharata where the Pando, a neighbouring tribe, claim to be members 
of the Pandav clan of Mahabharata (Surguja 2022).2 Other sources state that the name Korwa is 
derived from the term dodawas, meaning ‘earth diggers’ and their mother tongue is called by the 
same name (Singh 1994:613). Similarly, the name Kodaku is derived from Kodwa meaning ‘digger of 
the soil’ (1994:546).

The Korwa lived in and around the hills and forest for a long time, struggling for bare essentials 
such as food, clothing, and shelter. Gradually this situation became the basis for their simple 
lifestyle. This isolation forced them to develop their own means of survival. However, gradually their 
isolation has been broken and so has their identity. As a result of their contact with the outside 
world, their desire for further development is increasing (Mohan 1993:12–22).

The main staple of the Korwa and Kodaku is rice and wheat. They are not vegetarians. They eat 
a variety of leafy vegetables and pulses. Drinking an indigenous alcohol, called hadia, made from the 
mahua flower and fermented rice, as well as smoking and chewing tobacco are among their habits. 
They do not eat with other castes or tribes. However, they accept water and cooked food from 
neighbours such as the Yadav, Bania, Gond, Kanwar, and Kharwar (Singh 1994:547).

Based on the researchers’ compilation from different government documents from 2002–2005, 
the population of Korwa is estimated at 31,300 in Chhattisgarh (10,700 in Jashpur district and 
20,600 in Surguja district), and 18,400 in Jharkhand (excluding the population from Palamau and 
Gumla districts).

3 In the beginning of the 20th century, the Korwa tribe used to live in about 5–10 houses along the right bank land 
of Hasdeo river. At that time, this place was called Korwadih. Back then, India was divided into several kingdoms. 
The capital of Chhattisgarh was Ratanpur. With the permission of the king of Ratanpur, landlord Shri Ram Rai 
began to establish a colony which he renamed from Korwadih to Korba.

The Korwa people are mainly divided into two distinct groups, the Pahadi Korwa and the Dihari 
Korwa. The ones who still live in the hills and forest are called Pahadi/Pahariya Korwa (‘hill 
dwellers’) and the ones who came down and settled in the plain areas are called Dihari/Dihariya 
Korwa (‘plains dwellers’). They are not mutually dependent on each other. Their lifestyle, 
occupation, culture, etc. distinguish them as separate communities. The Dihari Korwa people live in a 
village situation, while the Pahadi Korwa people usually live in the? hills and forests. Occupationally, 
the Dihari Korwa people are agriculturists living in the plains, whereas the Pahadi Korwas people are 
food gatherers and basket makers who live in the hills, usually covered by dense forests (Narayan 
1990:18). The Dihari Korwa people are developed farmers and economically stabilized, while the 
Pahadi Korwa people are still economically poor.

In this study, the main focus is given to the Pahadi Korwa people group and their language. 
Socially, the Pahadi Korwa people are divided into five totemist endogamous clans which they call 
Gotra, with a specific totem for each:4 Hazeda ‘bamboo’, Edigwar-Kachi ‘a creeper’, Samat ‘a tree’, 
Madhiya-Dohs ‘head’, and Ginu ‘ant hill soil’ (CTDP 2002:n.p.). It is forbidden to marry within the 
same clan or with another caste, and Pahadi Korwa and Dihari Korwa do not intermarry. The system 
of bride price, remarriage, child marriage, and polygyny is commonly practiced.

Korwa marriage practices are typical for India (J.P., p.c. 2004). First, the bridegroom proposes 
to the bride’s family members. Agreeing to a proposal is called mangni. If the date is fixed, after few 
weeks or months, there is a feast known as Hadia, during which they drink the hadia beverage. Then, 
after fifteen days another feast is held, called Panchbandhi. On this occasion, the families decide to 
conduct the marriage on a particular day determined to be an auspicious or “lucky day” for 
marriage. According to custom, the marriage is conducted in the bride’s house. On the day of the 
wedding, there is a puja path (‘ritual’) called Pitra Puja. Following that there is a feast and a 
celebration which includes applying turmeric to each other and dancing while singing a traditional 
marriage song in the Korwa language. After the wedding, there is a programme called Chuman, 
during which all their relatives give the newlyweds clothes, household vessels, etc. After that 
programme the newlyweds go to the groom’s house.

Marriage is generally arranged through negotiation, by mutual consent. They mostly practise 
monogamy; however polygamy is also practiced by some people. A bride price is required, which is 
paid to the bride’s parents in cash and goods. One of the marriage rituals is to circle around the fire 
five times. Divorce can be sought by either spouse on grounds of barrenness or adultery. There is no 
bar for remarriage for either the man or the woman (Singh 1994:546).

Among the Kodaku both nuclear and extended families are found. In the family, they recognize 
birth purification, a ceremony that lasts for one day. The naming ceremony called chatti is celebrated 
on the sixth day. They also practice death purification, which they observe for ten days. The dead are 
generally buried, although they are sometimes cremated (J.P., p.c. 2004).

According to Singh’s (1994) study of different census data (1961–1981), more than 98 percent 
of the Korwa people are categorised under Hinduism while the remaining 2 percent belong to other 
religions. Another source reports that almost 70 percent of Korwa are followers of Hinduism, while 
another 29 percent are Muslim and 1 percent are Christian (Bethany World Prayer Center 1997). The 
traditional religion of these people groups may be considered to be animism, as they worship nature 
and their ancestors, whom they believe to be their providers and protectors. In the case of Kodaku 
people, the researchers observed that most of them practice Hinduism, but there now seems to be a 
high percentage of Christians.

use, attitude, and vitality. These questions were administered to mother tongue speakers in different 
villages. The subjects’ responses for each language are compiled. In addition, there were the informal 
interviews held and the observations made during fieldwork. (See Appendix A.)

A couple of questions in relation to language use were administered in Kotagohna, a Dihari Korwa 
village. Out of 19 subjects, all subjects reported that they widely use Sadri (or Surguja, an alternative 
name). In fact, the respondents reported Sadri as their mother tongue, and that they use it in every 
sphere of communication. A few respondents also stated that their children use Hindi in school. The 
researchers’ observations also concur with the subjects’ responses that the Dihari Korwa people do 
not have a separate mother tongue called Korwa.

Apart from the above responses, other answers reflect the respondents’ attitudes toward their 
language. A question, ‘If young people in your village did not speak Korwa, how would you feel?’, 
was asked to both young and old subjects. Among Speaking Pahadi Korwa, most older subjects 
expressed that they would be unhappy if their young people did not speak their language. Young 
people also responded that older people feel bad if they do not speak the Korwa language. On the 
other hand, when this same question was asked among Shifting Pahadi Korwa, the response suggest 
that it does not bother the old people whether their young people speak the Korwa language or not. 
In fact, one 80-year-old subject expressed that he is not sad for young people who are not able to 
speak the Korwa language because he himself does not know how to speak the language. Overall 
observations supported this finding.

The question ‘What is your mother tongue, and did your forefathers have a different language than 
what you speak today?’ was asked to find out whether the Dihari Korwa respondents perceive any 
significant linguistic relation to Pahadi Korwa. All subjects reported Sadri to be their mother tongue, 
and they exclaimed that their forefathers never had a different language other than Sadri. In 
addition, almost all respondents expressed that their favourite language is their mother tongue 
(Sadri), and that it is good and pure.

The responses to the question ‘If young people in your village do not speak Sadri, how would 
the old people feel?’ indicate that almost all the old subjects would be unhappy. For a few of them it 
does not matter, however. Young subjects all felt that the old people would feel unhappy if they do 
not speak Sadri, their mother tongue. Similarly, more than three-quarters of the total subjects 
reported that they will be unhappy if their children speak only Hindi, but all of them reported that 
they will be happy if their children read and write in their mother tongue, Sadri. In addition, when 
asked if the coming generations would continue to speak the language, all except one respondent 
said that they will surely speak their mother tongue.

The summary of the language use pattern among Kodaku respondents differs from state to state. A 
questionnaire was administered to a total of 85 subjects, out of which 44 subjects were from 
Chhattisgarh and 41 from Jharkhand. People in Jharkhand call their language Korwa instead of 
Kodaku (see section 1.4). Therefore, the results presented in this section include the responses that 
called their mother tongue Korwa.

In the questionnaire, a few questions were included to explore respondents’ attitudes  toward their 
mother tongue and other languages. As in the language use study, a total of 85 subjects, 44 from 
Chhattisgarh and 41 from Jharkhand, gave responses. A summary of their responses is analysed in

The Kodaku Marriage story from Kanda village shows a high average score (92%) with a low 
standard deviation (7), which indicates that most testees in Chakri village understood the story. On 
the other hand, the Korwa Job story from Rakkaya village shows a low average score (63%) with a 
high standard deviation (18), which demonstrates that many testees did not understand the story, 
and only a few were able to answer correctly.

Responses to the post-RTT questionnaire supports the above result. The testees reported that the 
Marriage story is in their language and that they understood it very well, d whereas the Job story is 
in a different variety which they could not understand well.

The findings of the lexical similarity study also indicate that Korwa and Kodaku are different 
languages. There is an issue, however, regarding the use of autonyms: Korwa is the term used most 
widely in Jharkhand for both the Korwa and the Kodaku people and their languages.

The ability to speak and understand two languages is called bilingualism. Blair (1990) says it is the 
knowledge and skills acquired by individuals, which enable them to use a second language other 
than their mother tongue. A second language may be acquired either formally (as in a school setting) 
or informally (through other types of contact). Bilingual proficiency, however, is not uniformly 
distributed within a community, as the level of proficiency varies among individuals and segments of 
the community (1990:52). It is closely related to demographic factors such as education, gender, age, 
and amount of travel, and depends upon their motivation and on the nature and extent of their 
contact with the second language.

The variety of Sadri spoken in Jharkhand and Orissa is being promoted and developed. People 
often consider this variety to be the standard. Abraham (1995:11) reports that the language 
development efforts in the Sadri language have been widespread; there is literature available in this 
variety. Sadri speakers, as well as the researchers, reported seeing Sadri books, listening to Sadri 
language cassettes and CDs, and hearing radio programs in Sadri. Books written in the Sadri 
language include an English-Sadri dictionary (Blain 1975), religious books, history books, especially 
developed in Jharsuguda or Rourkela, Orissa. There is a Sadri radio program which broadcasts from 
Ranchi, Jharkhand. According to Masica (1991:442), “Sadri language development is expected to 
continue. It is particularly active in Ranchi, Jharkhand, where the Sadri language is offered as a 
subject at the University of Ranchi.” Furthermore, in this modern age, media (audio and video) have 
played a significant role in propagating the wide use of Sadri. With these factors in mind, the 
researchers determined they should investigate Sadri bilingualism rather than Hindi bilingualism.

For bilingualism testing, the primary method is the sentence repetition test (SRT). However, since a 
Sadri SRT has not been developed, the researchers opted to use the RTT for exploring Sadri 
bilingualism among Korwa and Kodaku speakers. An RTT, however, is used to discern the 
intelligibility among related speech varieties. It is not a common method for testing bilingualism as it 
cannot determine bilingual proficiency at higher levels; at the most, it can confirm low proficiency 
levels. In addition to the RTT, a few questions regarding testees’ self-reported abilities in Sadri were 
included as part of the post-RTT questionnaire. The researchers’ observations in the field also helped 
to evaluate Sadri bilingualism levels among the Korwa and Kodaku groups.

An RTT can be used to provide a preliminary assessment of a community’s abilities in a second 
language. The procedures for evaluating testees’ bilingual abilities using this method are the same as 
those used for a dialect intelligibility testing. As this method only evaluates the comprehension 
ability of simple narratives, it is not adequate for evaluating higher levels of bilingual proficiency 
(Blair 1990:74).

Since the results of field-administered methods cannot be completely isolated from potential 
biases, O’Leary (1994) recommends that RTT results not be interpreted in terms of fixed numerical 
thresholds but rather be evaluated in light of other indicators of intelligibility such as lexical 
similarity, dialect opinions, and reported patterns of contact and communication (1994:48–72). In 
general, however, RTT mean scores of around 80 percent or higher with accompanying low standard 
deviations (usually 10 and below; high standard deviations are about 15 and above) may be taken to

indicate that respondents of the test point dialect display adequate understanding of the speech 
variety of the recorded text. Conversely, RTT means below around 60 percent are interpreted to 
indicate inadequate comprehension.

The fifth text, a Sadri story, called School story, was collected from Delatolli village in Ranchi, 
Jharkhand, during a previous survey (Abraham 1995). This variety of Sadri is said to be the standard 
Sadri variety and geographically closer to Korwa region. The surveyors tried using this story to test 
Sadri comprehension levels among Pahadi Korwa speakers.

After having tested eight subjects, however, the testing was discontinued. Because the quality of 
the recording was not good and because testees found the story difficult to understand, they seemed 
to lose interest in the test. They showed little patience with the testing procedures and achieved only 
very low scores.7

It was found that the Sadri variety spoken in the Pahadi Korwa region is different from that of 
Ranchi. Therefore, the researchers decided that the local Sadri variety spoken in the Pahadi Korwa 
region should be tested instead to explore Sadri comprehension levels. For that purpose, Dumortoli 
village, which is situated around five kilometres from Bagicha town in Jashpur district, was chosen 
as a reference point. Here a test called Life story was recorded from a mother tongue speaker of 
Sadri; to validate the test it was also hometown-tested in Dumortoli.

This local Sadri RTT from Dumortoli was used for Sadri comprehension testing in Rakkaya 
village. This village is situated around twelve kilometres from Sankargarh town in Surguja district. 
The wordlist from this village is the one that shares the highest lexical similarity percentages with 
the other Korwa wordlists. A Pahadi Korwa story (called Job story) was developed in this village and 
used as a practice story before the local Sadri story was played.

In addition to the local Sadri text, a story in standard Sadri (the Brave Hunter story) was used 
for Sadri comprehension testing. This story had also been collected during  the mentioned, previous 
survey, namely in Kesramal village in Rourkela, Orissa (Abraham 1995:App C-11). This Sadri RTT 
was tested in Kotagohna, a Dihari Korwa settlement, to test comprehension of standard Sadri. The 
Life story in local Sadri was used as a practice story since the Sadri spoken in Kotagohna is similar to 
that spoken in Dumortoli village.

The Pahadi Korwa Job story scored a high average of 94 percent, with a low standard deviation of 7. 
Post-HTT responses suggest that the language used in this text is good and pure with no mixing of 
other languages.

The local Sadri story achieved a high average score of 97 percent, with low standard deviation 
of 4. These results, together with the post-HTT responses, indicate that the local Sadri RTT is suitable 
for Sadri comprehension testing among Korwa speakers in different locations. All the subjects 
reported that the language used in this story was good and pure Sadri with no mixing of other 
languages. This story was also tested among the Dihari Korwa, which averaged 97%, with a low 
standard deviation of 6. In their post-HTT responses, the subjects stated that this story is in their own 
language.

The Kodaku Marriage story scored a high average of 97 percent, with a low standard deviation 
of 4. According to the post-HTT responses, that the language used in this story is good and pure with 
no mixing of other languages.

The RTT results for the Life story in local Sadri among the Pahadi Korwa testees show an average 
score of 88 percent, with a standard deviation of 12. This indicates that many testees were able to 
understand the story, while a few had difficulties. In other words, the Pahadi Korwa respondents at 
this test point display an adequate understanding of the local Sadri story. Considering the self-
reported questionnaires, those Pahadi Korwa who have more contact with outsiders generally are 
able to handle local Sadri. This category of people basically refers to the men, who generally learned 
the second language from outsiders. Two-thirds of the subjects who participated in the test were 
male.

The RTT results for the Brave Hunter story in standard Sadri among the Dihari Korwa show an 
average score of 86 percent, with a low standard deviation of 8. These results suggest that many 
Dihari Korwa testees understood the story well but that a few had difficulties. The post-RTT 
responses show that almost all the subjects understood the story. The testees also report that this text 
is in the Sadri variety which is spoken in Jharkhand and Orissa side. There is a little difference 
between this variety and their own, the local Sadri, they added.

The RTT result for the Brave Hunter story in standard Sadri among the Kodaku testees show an 
average score of 73 percent with a standard deviation of 13. This indicates that many testees could 
not understand the story well, but that a few are able to answer correctly. The post-RTT responses 
and observations support the fact that Kodaku people are not good at using standard Sadri. On the 
other hand, most of them reported the ability to handle the local Sadri very well. However, 
researchers did not test local Sadri comprehension among the Kodaku people to confirm this.

The Pahadi Korwa subjects (who were mostly male) were able to understand the recorded story 
in local Sadri. However, because it is fairly easy to pass an RTT without a high level of proficiency in 
the L2, it is not possible to draw any conclusions as to how proficient in Sadri those subjects are who 
achieved high comprehension scores.

The Dihari Korwa subjects speak a local variety of Sadri as their mother tongue. The subjects 
understood the standard Sadri story well. They identified the RTT Sadri variety as the one spoken in 
Jharkhand and Orissa side; they also submitted that this variety is only a little different from their 
own.

The Kodaku subjects had a low level of understanding of the standard Sadri story. Most subjects 
reported, however, to understand local Sadri well, but no testing was done to confirm this.

Among the Korwa: The Pahadi Korwa subjects, mostly male, were able to understand the 
recorded story in local Sadri. Given the limitations of the RTT methodology, however, no conclusions 
can be drawn as to how bilingual these subjects are in Sadri. The Dihari Korwa people speak a local 
variety of Sadri as their mother tongue. The testees understood the recorded text in standard Sadri 
well, maintaining that standard Sadri is only a little different from local Sadri.

A standardised list of 210 vocabulary items was collected from speakers at key locations for each of 
the language varieties studied in this survey. In standard procedure, the 210 words are elicited from 
a person who has grown up in the target locality. Ideally, the list is then collected a second time from 
another speaker at the same site. Any differences in responses are examined in order to identify 
(1) inaccurate responses due to misunderstanding of the elicitation cue, (2) loan words offered in 
response to the language of elicitation when indigenous terms are actually still in use, and (3) terms 
which are at different places along the generic-specific lexical scale. Normally, a single term is 
recorded for each item of the wordlist. However, more than one term is recorded for a single item 
when more than one specific term occupies the semantic area of a more generic item on the wordlist.

The extent to which speakers of related linguistic varieties understand one another can be 
studied by means of tape-recorded texts. Such studies investigate whether speakers of one variety 
understand a narrative text of another variety and are able to answer questions about the content of 
that text. The accuracy with which subjects answer these questions is taken as an index of their 
comprehension of that speech form. From the percentage of correct answers, the amount of 
intelligibility between speech forms is inferred. The RTT procedures followed in this survey are based 
on the procedures described in Casad (1974) and Blair (1990).

Short, personal experience narratives are deemed to be most suitable for recorded text testing in 
that the content must be relatively unpredictable and the speech form should be natural. Folklore or 
other material thought to be widely known is avoided. A three-to-five-minute story is recorded from 
a speaker of the regional vernacular and then checked with a group of speakers from the same region 
to ensure that the spoken forms are truly representative of that area. The story is then transcribed 
and a set of comprehension questions is constructed based on various semantic domains covered in 
the text. Normally, a set of fifteen or more questions is initially prepared. Some of the questions will 
prove unsuitable – perhaps because the answer is not in focus in the text, or because the question is 
confusing to native speakers of the test variety. Unsuitable questions are then deleted from the 
preliminary set, leaving a minimum of ten final questions for each RTT. To ensure that measures of 
comprehension are based on the subjects’ understanding of the text itself and not on a 
misunderstanding of the test questions, these questions must be recorded in the regional variety of 
the test subjects. This requires an appropriate dialect version of the questions for each RTT at each 
test location.

In the RTTs used in this study, test subjects heard the complete story text once, after which the 
story was repeated with the inserted test questions. . Each question was followed by a pause to give 
the testees the opportunity to respond. Appropriate and correct responses are directly extractable 
from the segment of speech immediately preceding the question, such that memory limitations exert 
a negligible effect and indirect inference based on the content is not required. Thus, the RTT aims to 
be a close reflection of a subject’s comprehension of the text, and by inference, of the language itself, 
and not of his or her memory, intelligence, or reasoning. The average or mean of the scores obtained 
from subjects at one test location is taken as a numerical indicator of the intelligibility between 
speakers of the dialects represented.

It is possible that a subject may be unable to answer the test questions correctly simply because 
he or she does not understand what is expected. This is especially true with unsophisticated subjects 
or those unacquainted with test-taking. Therefore, a very short pretest story with four questions is 
recorded in the local variety before beginning the actual testing. The purpose of this pretest is to 
teach the subject what is expected according to the RTT procedures. If the subject is able to answer 
the pretest questions, it is assumed that he or she would serve as a suitable subject. Each subject then 
participates in the HTT in his or her native variety before participating in RTTs in nonnative 
varieties. Occasionally, even after the pretest, a subject fails to perform adequately on an already 
validated HTT. Performances of such subjects are eliminated from the final evaluation, the 
assumption being that uncontrollable factors unrelated to the intelligibility of speech forms are

In contrast to experimentally controlled testing in a laboratory or classroom situation, the 
results of field-administered methods such as the RTT cannot be completely isolated from potential 
biases. Recorded texts and test questions will vary in terms of their relative difficulty and complexity, 
or of the clarity of the recording. Comparisons of RTT results from different texts need to be made 
cautiously. It is therefore recommended that results from RTTs not be interpreted in terms of fixed 
numerical thresholds, but rather be evaluated in light of other indicators of intelligibility such as 
lexical similarity, dialect opinions, and reported patterns of contact and communication. In general, 
however, RTT mean scores of around 80 percent or higher with accompanying low standard 
deviations are usually taken to indicate that respondents of the test point dialect display adequate 
understanding of the variety represented by the recording. Conversely, RTT means below 60 percent 
are interpreted to indicate inadequate intelligibility.
